chapter.name: Exploring Magnets
chapter.blurb: Reshma's story of sailors lost without stars introduces the magnetic compass, launching an exploration of magnetic and non-magnetic materials, a magnet's paired poles regardless of its shape, why a freely suspended magnet always settles north-south because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, the construction and history (including the Indian matsya-yantra) of the magnetic compass, the attraction/repulsion rule and why only repulsion proves an object is a magnet, and how the magnetic effect passes through non-magnetic materials such as wood, cardboard, plastic and glass.

scope_in.item: Classify materials as magnetic (attracted to a magnet, e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their metal combinations) or non-magnetic (not attracted, e.g. wood, rubber)
Locate a magnet's two poles (North and South) as the ends where iron filings cluster most; poles always exist in pairs, even in the smallest broken piece, so a single pole cannot be obtained
Recognise that magnets of different shapes (bar, U-shaped, ring, disc, cylindrical, spherical) and both natural magnets (lodestones) and artificial (iron-based) magnets all have exactly two poles

Explain why a freely suspended magnet always comes to rest along the north-south direction because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, and use this to test whether an unmarked bar is a magnet
Describe the construction and use of a magnetic compass (needle mounted freely on a pin, red north-seeking end, dial, rotating the box to align markings with the needle)
Know the historical Indian navigation device, the matsya-yantra (a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece in a vessel of oil), as a precursor of the modern compass
Make a simple compass by magnetising a sewing needle (stroking with one pole of a magnet, in a single direction, 30-40 times), testing it with iron filings, and floating it on a cork in water
State and apply the rule that like poles (North-North, South-South) repel and unlike poles (North-South) attract

Identify that a magnet can be distinguished from a plain magnetic material (e.g. iron) only by the property of repulsion, since a plain iron bar is attracted by both poles of a magnet but never repels one
Use a compass needle's deflection (moving away for like poles, moving closer for unlike poles) to identify or test the poles of an unmarked magnet
Explain that the magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials, demonstrated with wood, cardboard, plastic and glass sheets placed between a magnet and a compass needle

Apply attraction/repulsion and magnetism-through-non-magnetic-materials to explain simple magnet-based tricks and toys (magnetic garland, steel balls in a maze moved via a cardboard tray, retrieving a paperclip from water, matchbox cars with facing magnets)

Know the safe-storage rule for magnets: store in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, a wooden piece between them, and soft-iron keeper pieces across the ends, and general care such as avoiding heat, dropping, hammering, and keeping magnets near mobile phones or remote controls

concepts.name: Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
concepts.description: Classifying materials as magnetic (attracted to a magnet) or non-magnetic (not attracted), based on Activity 4.1 and the magnetic metals named in the chapter.
concepts.idea: Some materials are pulled towards a magnet and some are not.
concepts.rule: Materials that are attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials; iron is the most common example, and nickel and cobalt are also magnetic metals, as are some of their combinations with other metals. Materials that are not attracted towards a magnet, such as wood and rubber, are called non-magnetic materials. Bringing a magnet near an object and observing whether it sticks tells us which group the object belongs to.
concepts.example: A pencil (wood) and an eraser (rubber) do not stick to a magnet, so they are non-magnetic materials.

concepts.name: Poles of a Magnet
concepts.description: Locating a magnet's two poles where iron filings cluster most, the impossibility of a single pole, and how this holds for magnets of every shape and origin.
concepts.idea: Every magnet, whatever its shape, has exactly two poles that always exist in pairs.
concepts.rule: Iron filings sprinkled near a magnet stick mostly at its two ends, and very little at the rest of the magnet; these ends are called the poles of the magnet, named the North pole and the South pole. It is not possible to obtain a magnet with a single pole: even if a magnet is broken into smaller pieces, each piece is itself a complete magnet with its own North and South pole. This is true whatever the magnet's shape - bar, U-shaped, ring, disc, cylindrical or spherical - and whether the magnet is a naturally occurring lodestone or an artificial magnet made from iron.
concepts.example: When a bar magnet is tapped over paper sprinkled with iron filings, most filings cluster near its two ends, showing where its poles are.

concepts.name: Finding Directions: the Freely Suspended Magnet
concepts.description: Why a freely suspended magnet always settles north-south, and using this to test whether an unmarked bar is a magnet.
concepts.idea: A magnet, freely suspended, always settles pointing north-south because the Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.
concepts.rule: If a bar magnet is suspended by a thread tied at its middle so that it can rotate freely, it will always come to rest along the north-south direction, however many times the experiment is repeated. This happens because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. The end of the magnet that points north is called the North-seeking pole, or North pole, and the end pointing south is the South-seeking pole, or South pole. Repeating the activity with a plain iron bar instead of a magnet does not give this consistent result - it can come to rest along any direction - so this property can be used to test whether an unmarked piece of metal is truly a magnet.
concepts.example: A bar magnet hung freely by a thread always swings back to point north-south, while a similarly hung plain iron bar does not.

concepts.name: The Magnetic Compass
concepts.description: The construction and use of a magnetic compass, the historical Indian matsya-yantra, and building a simple compass by hand.
concepts.idea: A magnetic compass uses a freely-pivoted needle-magnet to show directions, and can even be built by hand.
concepts.rule: A magnetic compass has a magnet in the shape of a needle, mounted on a pin so that it can rotate freely inside a small box with a dial marked with directions; the north-seeking end of the needle is usually painted red. To find directions, the compass is placed down and the needle allowed to come to rest along north-south, then the box is gently rotated until the North and South marks on the dial line up with the needle; all other directions can then be read off the dial. A similar, much older Indian device called the matsya-yantra used a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece floating in a vessel of oil to find directions at sea. A simple compass can even be made by magnetising an iron sewing needle - stroking it repeatedly with one pole of a bar magnet in a single direction - and floating it, passed through a cork, in a bowl of water.
concepts.example: Passing a magnetised needle through a cork and floating it in water lets it turn freely and settle pointing north-south, just like a real compass needle.

concepts.name: Attraction, Repulsion, and Identifying a Magnet
concepts.description: The like-repel, unlike-attract rule between magnets, and why only repulsion can prove for certain that an object is a magnet.
concepts.idea: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and only this repulsion can prove that an object is really a magnet.
concepts.rule: When two magnets are brought close together, their like poles (North-North or South-South) repel each other, while their unlike poles (North-South) attract each other. If one of the two objects is replaced by a plain iron bar instead of a magnet, both ends of the iron bar are attracted by both poles of the magnet - the iron bar never repels. This means that attraction alone cannot prove an object is a magnet, since a magnet attracts plain magnetic materials too; only repulsion is possible exclusively between two magnets, so the property of repulsion is used to identify a magnet for certain. The same like-repel, unlike-attract rule applies to a compass needle, since the needle is itself a small magnet. Magnets should also be stored carefully, in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, with a wooden piece between them and soft iron pieces across the ends, and kept away from heat, hard knocks, and devices like mobile phones.
concepts.example: Bringing the North pole of a bar magnet near the North pole of a compass needle makes the needle swing away, since like poles repel.

concepts.name: Magnetism Acts Through Non-magnetic Materials
concepts.description: Activity 4.7 shows the magnetic effect passes through non-magnetic sheets, explaining several magnet tricks in the chapter.
concepts.idea: A magnet's pull can act through a non-magnetic material placed in its way.
concepts.rule: When a sheet of a non-magnetic material - wood, cardboard, plastic or glass - is placed between a magnet and a compass needle, there is no appreciable change in how much the needle deflects; the magnetic effect passes through these non-magnetic materials nearly as if they were not there. This explains tricks such as picking a steel paperclip out of a bowl of water using a magnet held outside the bowl without wetting the magnet or your fingers, or moving steel balls out of a maze by sliding a magnet underneath a cardboard tray.
concepts.example: A magnet moved outside a glass of water can still pull a steel paperclip resting inside the water towards the glass wall.
